title: Not “suffering”
told: a story from the Buddhist commentaries

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever felt like the only one going through something hard?
options: i’m so sorry. you’re less alone than it feels. listen.
then this woman will feel familiar. listen.
i’m glad. keep this one for someone who does.

steps.line: In the city of Savatthi lived a young mother named Kisa Gotami. When her little son died, she could not accept it.
She went from house to house, asking everyone for medicine to bring him back. People pitied her. Nobody could help.
At last someone sent her to the Buddha. “I know a medicine,” he said gently. “Bring me a handful of mustard seeds.”

steps.q: There’s one condition. What do you think it is?
o: Picked at dawn, by her own hand
From a house where no one has died
Paid for with her own savings
steps.why: Mustard seed was in every kitchen. A house that had never known a death was not.

steps.line: “But they must come from a house where no one has ever died.” Glad, she hurried back into the town.
At every door, people gladly held out seeds. Then she asked her question. “The living are few,” they said, “but the dead are many.”

steps.q: Why send her for seeds, instead of just telling her that death comes to everyone?
o: To keep her busy until the pain faded
He had no real medicine to offer
She needed to see it for herself
steps.why: She had to find it out herself. By the last door, it wasn’t a lesson anymore. It was what she knew.

steps.line: By evening she understood. Not one house was untouched. Her grief was real, and it was not hers alone.

steps.q: Night falls. Not one house can give her the seeds. What does Gotami do?
o: Keeps knocking, into the next town
Gives up and goes home in despair
Stops searching and lays her son to rest
steps.why: She took her son to the charnel ground, the old commentary says, and went back to the Buddha. The search ended because she finally understood, not because she failed.

steps.line: She laid her son to rest and went back to the Buddha, her hands empty. Later she became a nun, remembered as one who woke up.

steps.q: Gotami comes back to the Buddha with empty hands. Why does the story count that as the cure?
o: She no longer needed the impossible thing
She had finally stopped grieving him
She was too tired to keep searching
steps.why: Nothing brought her son back, and her grief was real. What healed was letting go of the fight against his death. Her own verses survive among the poems of the first Buddhist nuns, the Therigatha.

steps.line: Today, someone tells a friend what’s been hard. The friend says, “Me too.” Nothing is fixed. But the wobble is shared.
steps.label: today

say: the buddha’s first big word is dukkha. it’s usually translated “suffering,” but it’s wider than that: plain pain, yes, and also the ache of good things changing, and a quiet wobble under even good days.

one popular picture splits the word: du, bad, and kha, the hole where a wheel’s axle goes. the cart still rolls, with a little jolt every turn. seeing it clearly is often a relief. it’s not just me. it’s the wheel.

steps.q: You’re on the best holiday of your life. Where’s the dukkha in that?
o: There isn’t any, that’s the point
It’s already ending, and part of you knows
steps.why: Teachers call this the dukkha of change: even good things wobble because they don’t last. The Buddha named it alongside plain pain.

steps.q: In that old picture, du means bad and su means good. So what did su-kha, the well-fitted axle hole, come to mean?
steps.why: A wheel that turns without a jolt. Sukha is an everyday Pali word for happiness and ease. The axle picture is a teacher’s favorite, though language scholars debate whether that’s really where the word comes from.

today.say: when something wobbles today, a late train, a hard message, a tight shoulder, don’t fix it right away. just name it quietly: “this too.” buddhist teachers call this seeing the first truth.
options: this too. that’s the whole practice.
that counts. gotami needed a whole day of doors.

sources: Dhammapada Commentary, the story of Kisa Gotami (on Dhammapada 114): her dead son, the search for medicine, the mustard seed from a house where no one has died, “the living are few, but the dead are many”
Therigatha Commentary on Kisa Gotami (Therigatha 10.1); her verses in Therigatha 10.1; her ordination and awakening
Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11): dukkha as the first noble truth
Dukkhata Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 45.165): three kinds of dukkha (pain, change, conditioned existence)
du + kha (“bad axle hole”) and su + kha: a popular teaching explanation, not settled etymology
check: “The living are few, but the dead are many” follows Burlingame’s English of the Dhammapada Commentary; confirm wording.
The du/kha axle-hole etymology is a popular teaching picture that scholars dispute; the lesson calls it “one popular picture.”
Details differ between the Dhammapada and Therigatha commentaries (e.g. where she laid her son to rest, and the lamp episode, left out here).
